1:
Two voices open by explaining why the letter is angry. Chrysostom says the cause cannot have been slight, since to be exasperated by common matters is the part of the little-minded: what roused Paul was an offence estranging the Galatians from Christ. Certain Jewish believers, held by the prepossessions of Judaism and intoxicated by vain-glory, had taught that circumcision, sabbaths and new moons must be kept, claiming that Peter, James and John did not forbid them — which Chrysostom grants, but explains as condescension to Jewish weakness, a condescension Paul had no need of among Gentiles though he used it himself in Judaea. Luther gives the same occasion differently: false teachers crept in after Paul's departure and overthrew what he had planted, men of standing who boasted of the holy stock, the promises and the fathers, and who asked the Galatians why they esteemed a man converted last of all, who had never seen Christ and had persecuted the Church. Barnes and Clarke preface the chapter instead with the history of the province, deriving its name from the Gauls who invaded Asia Minor and settled there and citing the same authorities for the mixed population that made it Gallograecia; Barnes then sets out the chapter as one argument, that Paul was not appointed, commissioned or taught by men, and that when the apostles at Jerusalem did learn his views they fully concurred.

On the title Calvin is most exact. Paul claims it to employ the authority of his station in enforcing his doctrine, an authority depending not on the judgment of men but on the calling of God; in the church we listen to God alone, and whoever assumes a right to instruct us must speak in his name. Calvin notes that the calumniators refused him only the name and rank of apostle, not the honour of the ministry, and that the word is used two ways — of preachers generally, and here of the highest rank, so that Paul stands equal to Peter and the Twelve. Ellicott fills in the wider use, under which Barnabas and James the Lord's brother were also called apostles. Gill adds that Paul neither took the honour to himself nor ran before he was sent; Henry insists this was no common call of an ordinary minister but an extraordinary call from heaven, neither qualification nor designation coming by human mediation; and Wesley observes that Paul is elsewhere modest with the title, omitting it where others are joined in the salutation, where he writes of secular affairs, and to the Hebrews, since he was not properly their apostle.

The two prepositions carry the argument. Ellicott separates them — not of men marks the source from which authority derives, neither by man the channel through which it is conveyed, as we call the sovereign the fount of honour though the ministry confers it in her name — and applies it to the two obvious objections: Ananias's part was too subordinate to introduce a human element, and the separation at Antioch assigned a sphere rather than conferred an office. Robertson explains the bluntness from the charge that Paul was no genuine apostle because not one of the Twelve, and takes the closing clause as the qualification itself: he could be an apostle because he had seen the Risen Christ. Wesley says the same more shortly: bearing witness to the resurrection was the peculiar business of an apostle. Cyril, on the raising, strings together the testimonies to Christ's session at the right hand from the Gospel, from Peter and from Paul's letters. Tertullian turns the verse round entirely. Arguing against Marcion, he demands the origin of an apostle he cannot find in the Gospel's catalogue, and says that a choice made after Christ had attained his rest in heaven imputes improvidence to Christ, as though he were added by fortuitous encounter rather than deliberate selection.
2:
Why Paul joins all the brethren to his name is disputed. Calvin says he wrote in the name of many because those who might attach less weight to a solitary individual would listen to a greater number; his usual practice is to put salutations at the end and name no more than two, so including them all here is the opposite method, adopted because the concurrence of so many godly persons must have softened them. Ellicott denies that motive — Paul is ready enough to take the whole defence of his cause upon himself — and suggests only that he wished to show he had their sympathy. Luther turns the phrase into an argument, extending the first verse's distinction into three: the false apostles are sent of men or by men; Paul of God and not by man; the brethren of God, howbeit by man, that is by Paul himself — so they write as fellow-soldiers and not as apostles, witnesses that his doctrine is true.

Calling them churches troubles Calvin, since the word implies unity of faith and these had almost entirely revolted. His answer is that so long as they professed Christianity, worshipped one God and observed the sacraments, they kept the external marks of a church; the purest have their blemishes, and we are not instantly to pronounce a society's defects sufficient reason for withholding the name. Wesley notices the other half: Paul does not here call them saints, or elect, or churches of God, as he does elsewhere. Ellicott adds that the salutation is deliberately abrupt, Paul's custom being to begin with commendation and to find something to praise even at Corinth, whereas the Galatian error goes more to the root; Robertson observes that the letter is circular.

On the gift the voices divide between grammar and rhetoric. Ellicott separates the three Greek prepositions that English renders alike by for — concerning, used of things, in behalf of and in place of, used of persons — and concludes that the death was a sacrifice with respect to sins, on behalf of sinners, and in their stead. Robertson adds Lightfoot's judgement that the word for deliverance strikes the keynote of the epistle: the gospel is a rescue, an emancipation from bondage. Gill and Luther reach for the same figure and pile up what was not given: not the world and its fulness, not gold or silver, not men, not angels, but himself — his flesh, his blood, his whole human nature. Luther presses it on both sides, that Christ did not receive our works or the sacrifices of Moses's law, and did not give himself for a crown or a kingdom or for our holiness but for our sins — words he calls thunderclaps from heaven against every kind of righteousness. Barnes explains why the doctrine comes so early: it is cardinal, and the Galatians had let it be obscured, and the word gave shows the act was wholly voluntary.

The phrase this present evil world divides them. Clarke denies it can mean created nature or wicked men, and concludes that Paul means the Jews and their system of carnal ordinances, a burden neither they nor their fathers could bear — adding that on Schoettgen's account the adjective would better be rendered oppressive. Wesley and Robertson keep the general sense, Wesley taking it of the guilt, wickedness and misery the world is involved in, Robertson rendering it literally as the existing age, evil, with the adjective in the emphatic position. On the doxology Ellicott asks whether the word is the glory, the divine glory with which none can compare — in which case it would be better to supply is than be, since that glory already belongs to God and is not prayed for; and he takes for ages of ages as a Hebraism for infinite time, where Gill calls it a Jewish phrase.
6:
Three voices agree that the opening word is deliberately gentle, and one says where he got it. Barnes remarks that Paul uses as mild a word as possible, not severe reproof but astonishment, and credits the observation to Luther; Luther's own comment is that Paul does not at first set upon them with vehement words but after a very fatherly sort, in a manner excusing their fall, while reserving plain thunderings for the seducers on whom he lays the whole fault, his purpose being to raise up the fallen rather than crush them. Calvin says the same: the rebuke is milder than they deserved, the severity kept for the false apostles. Barnes draws a date from the same word: so soon shows the letter cannot have been long after the gospel first reached them, on the common supposition two to five years.

From whom they were removed is disputed. Clarke says the apostle seems here to mean himself, since it was he who called them. Henry says they were removed not only from the apostle who was the instrument but from God himself, who directed the preaching; Ellicott makes it flatly God the Father, to whom Paul always attributes the call, Christ's part being the mediate agency named next. Three voices stop at the tense. Ellicott notes that the Greek verb is the regular word for a deserter or turncoat, and that the tense is strictly present: you are at this moment in the act of falling away. Robertson renders it you are transferring yourselves. Calvin builds an exhortation on it — I do not yet say ye have been removed, for then it would be harder to return; but now, at the critical moment, do not advance a step, but instantly retreat. He adds that what they were leaving was Christ himself, the false teachers leaving them only an imaginary Christ, as the Papists have none because they will have a divided and mangled one.

What the rival message was divides them further. Clarke alone takes another gospel for an actual document, noting that spurious gospels circulated in the earliest ages, that their multitude induced Luke to write, that more than seventy names survive in Fabricius's collection, and that some urged circumcision and the Mosaic law — to one of these, he thinks, Paul refers. The rest take it as the Judaizing message. Robertson rests on the distinction between the two Greek words for other: these men preach another Jesus. Barnes, reviewing the older renderings from Tindale and Locke onward, settles for the sense that the thing had none of the characteristics of a gospel. Ellicott turns the conjunction into except that: the only sense in which a second gospel can be spoken of is that some are perverting the first, the verb meaning to reverse a thing into its opposite. Gill says it is no joyful sound and no good news, there being but one gospel, whose trumpet gives no uncertain sound; Wesley calls it heavy tidings rather than glad, setting acceptance with God on impossible terms, and reports the troublers' claim that the other apostles, and Paul himself, insisted on the law. Calvin says they do nothing but trouble and subvert, and that subversion is worse than corruption.

Tertullian reads the chapter from outside the quarrel. He grants that this epistle is the most decisive against Judaism and that the ancient law is abolished, but insists the abolition proceeds from the Creator's own dispensation, foretold by the prophets and dated by Christ at John the Baptist. His argument against Marcion is that the Galatian error proves the point: they thought faith in Christ obligatory without annulling the law precisely because they could not believe the law would be set aside by its own author — whereas had Paul preached another god, they would have concluded at once that the old god's law must go.
8:
The supposition is agreed to be impossible and the curse is not. Gill says no established apostle could preach another gospel, nor could a good angel be employed to publish one, and that if it were done the highest names would not screen the doer. Ellicott notes that the Greek marks an extreme and improbable case. Robertson puts it as a renegade's turn — the Jews had called Paul a renegade for leaving Judaism — and adds that no angel can change him now. Where they differ is on the anathema. Clarke would soften it: perhaps this is not an imprecation but a direction, that such a person have no countenance and, as Theodoret puts it, be put out of the Church's communion. Luther takes it at full force: Paul here excommunicates and curses all teachers in general — himself, his brethren, an angel, and every other — an exceeding great fervency of spirit. Cyril turns the verse to another use, making it the guarantee of the baptismal creed: hold only what the Church has delivered, engraved on the memory rather than written on paper, and receive no other — not if we ourselves should change and contradict our present teaching, nor if an adverse angel transformed into an angel of light should wish to lead you astray.

One small preposition carries a confessional weight, and Ellicott says so openly. The word rendered than that may mean besides or contrary to; the first sense has been favoured by Protestant and the second by Roman Catholic commentators, since one seems to exclude and the other to admit an appeal to tradition. Ellicott decides for contrary, since what the Judaizers offered was an opposition of principles and not an addition to the old. Calvin decides the other way: the false apostles' doctrine was not contrary to Paul's, nor even different, but corrupted by false additions.

Why the sentence is repeated occupies Barnes and Luther, and both notice the same alteration in it. The first curse falls on preaching other than we have preached, the second on other than ye have received. Luther says Paul does this on purpose, lest the Galatians answer that they had not perverted his gospel but merely misunderstood him; Barnes says the change reminds them they had once professed it, so that the new teachers contradict what the Galatians knew to be true. On the introductory words the two part company: Ellicott refers as we said before to Paul's second visit, when the germs of the apostasy would already be visible, while Barnes holds it cannot have been said while he was among them and takes it for as I have just said.

The last verse turns on a word that will not sit still. Gill takes persuade as teach, and finds it inapplicable to God without supplying something. Clarke and Ellicott make it court or conciliate, and Ellicott adds that yet means still, at this late period, Paul having cut himself adrift from his age too thoroughly to float with the tide. Robertson makes the tense conative, an attempt at persuading. Barnes reads now as marking the contrast with his life before conversion, when he did take his commission from men. Henry allows two senses: that Paul acted in obedience to God and not men, or that his aim was to bring others into that obedience. Luther supplies the tone: am I so unknown among you, when all men see that this preaching has earned me my own nation's hatred? Calvin finds two arguments, that Paul was not prompted by ambition to accommodate himself to men, and — far stronger — that he was not the author of the gospel but delivered faithfully what he had received. Wesley presses the alternative home: hear this, all who hope to keep in favour with God and the world at once.
11:
Two voices notice the address before the argument. Gill observes that after all their wandering Paul still calls them brethren, hoping well of them and using the word to engage attention; Wesley notices the opposite, that he does not give them even this appellation until now. Ellicott identifies the verb rendered certify as the one Paul uses for declaring and for giving to understand, reserved for statements made with emphasis and solemnity, and would render after man by an adjective — the gospel is not human, not to be judged by a human measure. Robertson gives the same sense and notices the play by which the gospel is the thing gospelled. Luther rules out a weaker reading: Paul does not mean merely that his gospel is not earthly, for that is manifest and the false apostles also bragged their doctrine was heavenly, but that he learned it by no earthly means at all, as the rest of us do, some by hearing, some by reading, some by writing. Clarke puts it that there is not a spark of human invention in it nor a touch of human cunning; Calvin calls this the hinge on which the whole question turns, and notes that Paul does not leave it an assertion but proves it from a narrative of facts.

Who might have taught him is the standing objection, and it has two quite different answers. Barnes states it plainly — the one plausible difficulty is the interview with Ananias — and gives three replies: no evidence that Ananias explained the religion, Paul already taught on the road to Damascus, and Ananias sent to restore sight and give the Spirit. Calvin concedes far more and denies that it matters: divine instruction by immediate inspiration did not make it improper that a man should be employed to teach him, if only to give weight to his public ministry. Gill sweeps the field instead, ruling out Gamaliel — from whom he had the law and the traditions but not a whit of the gospel, rather prejudices against it — then the apostles, whom he did not see for years, then Ananias and any other man. Robertson adds the university of Tarsus. Behind this Calvin sets the charge being answered: that Paul's gospel was defective and spurious, got from an inferior teacher, while his opponents boasted instruction from the highest apostles. Luther notes that Paul confirms the denial with an oath, so that the Galatians may believe him against men he treats as liars.

What the revelation was, and whether there was one, divides the last two. Ellicott argues that it must have come at or near the conversion, which excludes the later vision Paul reports elsewhere, and faces the difficulty that the Damascus appearance looks too brief to contain a sum of doctrine — answering that it held the two points from which all the rest flows, the Messiahship of Jesus and faith in him. Robertson denies the question needs settling in the singular: the aorist does not require one unveiling, Paul had numerous visions, and he uses the same verb of receiving the account of the Lord's Supper from the Lord. Wesley fills in the content — the resurrection, the ascension, the calling of the Gentiles and Paul's own apostleship, with the promise that Christ would appear again for other things. On the pair of verbs the two part company: Ellicott sets taught against revelation as process against gift, so that the first neither qualifies the pronoun rather than answering the second — the gospel is not human as it comes to you, nor was it human as it came to me — while Wesley distinguishes them by tempo, receiving being at once and being taught slowly. Clarke rests on the plain denial, adding that Paul was commissioned by Christ alone and had his knowledge from Christ crucified.
13:
How the Galatians came to know Paul's earlier life is answered four ways. Barnes supposes he had told them himself; Ellicott says the thing was notorious, but that Paul habitually brought his own career into his preaching; Gill offers both, and adds that they may have heard it from Jews of the dispersion, perhaps from some who had fled into Galatia on account of that very persecution; Clarke says they knew it because, being Jews, they knew what had happened in Judea. Calvin explains why it is here: the narrative is part of the argument, since a mortal enemy of the gospel could only have been converted by God, and Paul calls his readers as witnesses to a matter not in doubt. Luther gives it its edge — if the righteousness of the law had been worth anything, I should not have turned back from it; let them show me a more zealous defender of Moses's law than I was.

What Paul means by the traditions of his fathers divides the commentators two against four. Ellicott identifies them with the traditions of the elders that made the commandment of God of none effect, the oral law that grew up beside the Pentateuch and was afterwards embodied in the Mishnah; Wesley calls them the unwritten traditions, over and above those written in the law; Barnes says a large part of Pharisaic doctrine rested on mere tradition. Calvin denies it flatly: Paul means not the additions by which God's law had been corrupted but the law of God itself, in which he was educated from childhood. Luther agrees in terms — these are not pharisaical or human traditions but the holy law of Moses itself, received as an inheritance from the fathers. Clarke takes a narrower view of the boast: Paul claims not to have excelled his countrymen in the love and practice of the pure law of God but only to have been more skilled in the traditions than his fellow students, where Ellicott widens the progress to cover zeal and strictness of observance too.

The words themselves attract three notes. Robertson observes that Judaism occurs in the New Testament only here and in the next verse, coming in from Maccabees, where it names the Jewish religion as against the Hellenism the Syrian kings were pressing on the Jews, and that a later father coined Christianity on the pattern; Ellicott adds that the term carries no disparagement. On the word for wasting the church, Robertson notes that it means to lay waste or sack a city, and is the very word the Christians at Damascus used of Saul after his conversion, which Paul evidently heard and kept; Ellicott points to the same verb rendered destroyed there. On my equals both take it as equals in age, Ellicott picturing the young men who came up with Paul to study at the feet of Gamaliel, and comparing a public man looking back on his university contemporaries and his zealous advocacy of a cause long since abandoned.

Cyril stands apart and reads the persecution as providence. He professes wonder at the dispensation of the Spirit, who confined the letters of the rest to a small number and gave the former persecutor the privilege of writing fourteen — not because Peter or John was less, but so that the doctrine might be beyond question, and all thereby made believers. He then stages objection and answer: all were amazed and asked whether this was not the man who had come to lead them away bound to Jerusalem, and Paul replies that he is not worthy to be called an apostle, but that he did it in ignorance, thinking the preaching of Christ was the destruction of the Law and not knowing that Christ came to fulfil it. Gill keeps to the plain sense: the deeper he went into Judaism the more violent a persecutor he became.
15:
Ellicott settles the phrase about the womb against the reading most would expect: comparison with the other places where it occurs makes the sense from the moment of my birth rather than from before my birth. Barnes takes it as a purpose formed at birth rather than a call issued in infancy, and draws from it that a young man who has gone far astray may still be destined for holy work, as Paul, Newton, Bunyan and Augustine were. Wesley makes the parallel with Jeremiah and then concedes what an Arminian might be expected to resist: such an unconditional predestination as this may consist with God's justice and mercy alike. Robertson finds a pointed irony in the verb: it means to mark off from a boundary, and the Pharisees were precisely the separated ones, so Paul conceives himself a spiritual Pharisee, marked off now for the gospel.

Whether the Son was revealed in Paul or to him is the sharpest question here. Gill knows the readings by me and to me and prefers in him, an inward discovery in which Christ was formed in him and dwelt in his heart by faith. Ellicott agrees that it means in the mind or consciousness and builds a sequence on it: first the instantaneous flash of the idea on the soul, then the prolonged conflict and meditation in Arabia in which it was consolidated, and last the public preaching. Calvin decides the other way, taking the construction as a Hebrew idiom in which the particle is redundant, so that it means simply to me, and adding that Christ was revealed not that Paul might silently enjoy the knowledge but that he might preach it. Robertson also prefers in my case, following Lightfoot. Wesley refuses to choose, taking it of the Spirit's operation within and of the heavenly vision alike; Henry turns it into a warning, that it will little avail us to have Christ revealed to us if he is not also revealed in us.

On conferring with flesh and blood, Clarke explains the phrase as a Hebraism for any man whatever and rejects a favourite gloss outright — many suppose Paul means he did not consult the suggestions of his own unrenewed heart, but no such thing is intended by the text. Wesley states that very gloss as his own: Paul took no counsel with any man, nor with his own reason or inclinations, which might have raised numberless objections. Calvin keeps to the wider sense, that Paul would have nothing to do with human counsels of any kind; Robertson notes that the verb means to lay a matter on oneself in addition, and recurs only in the next chapter.

Arabia is a blank each fills differently. Barnes says it lay south of Damascus and admits that the part, the purpose and the length of stay are unknown. Clarke fixes it as the portion contiguous to Damascus, then under Aretas, and explains the silence of Acts by Luke's absence from the journey. Ellicott notes that the boundary was undefined and that some writers included Damascus itself, so the desert near the city is the obvious supposition — though he allows a certain appropriateness in the region of Sinai. Robertson places the journey between the two Damascus visits that Acts does not distinguish. On the three years Calvin answers the charge of inconsistency by saying Luke simply omits them; Gill harmonises instead, allowing that Paul may have gone up early, when he fell into a trance in the temple and was ordered away, but stayed no time and saw no apostle. Luther makes the narrative a confutation of the claim that Paul was merely a pupil of the apostles who had lived under the law; Calvin adds that naming the apostles separately implies no disrespect, since a creature compared with God has no ground of complaint.
18:
Nobody agrees from what the three years are counted. Barnes reckons from the departure for Damascus, not from the return out of Arabia, and says most commentators agree; Clarke allows either terminus; Calvin counts from the start of the apostolic office; Robertson calls it a round number. Ellicott takes it from the conversion and then unsettles the enterprise, pointing out that the phrase need not mean three full years — as the three days in the grave were not three full days — so that it may cover one year and parts of two, and that this ambiguity shows the difficulty of any precise chronology.

The verb rendered to see interests four of them. Barnes notes that it is not the ordinary word for seeing, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and means to ascertain by personal inquiry and then narrate, as an historian does — whence our word history. Clarke makes the same derivation and turns it into a complaint, that ninety-nine of every hundred of our histories show how far the word has fallen, being anything but true relations of facts and persons. Ellicott says the word belongs to sight-seeing, of places first and of persons after, and is used only of something notable; Paul's object was acquaintance with Peter as head of the community, not instruction. Robertson says he visited him as an equal. Clarke presses the negative: it was not to get religious knowledge, since Paul knew as much of the Jewish religion as Peter and had preached the gospel three years already. Calvin makes the short stay the argument, adding that Paul went deliberately, lest he be thought to be avoiding their society. Ellicott also settles the name — the true reading is Cephas, the commoner form having crept in — and again grants a point to the other side: Roman Catholic commentators argue from this passage, not without reason, that Peter had by then taken the lead in the Church.

Who James was divides them, and the division turns on whether he can be called an apostle. Barnes and Clarke both work from the two Jameses of the Acts, one killed by Herod and one remaining at Jerusalem, and both take brother for a near kinsman, Barnes citing Doddridge and Clarke citing Paley; Wesley glosses it as kinsman without argument. Calvin reports the tradition that this James was surnamed the Just and presided at Jerusalem, notes the rival views that he was Joseph's son by another wife or Christ's cousin, and rejects the last — otherwise, he says, the more probable — because he is here counted among the apostles, refusing Jerome's plea that the word is sometimes used more widely. Robertson agrees that he is termed an apostle here though not of the Twelve. Ellicott makes the apostleship depend on the identification rather than the reverse, and states his firm conviction that the theory identifying the Lord's brethren with his cousins cannot stand.

On the oath they differ about its scope. Barnes extends it to the whole group of facts in the chapter, and explains why an oath was needed: there were no witnesses to appeal to, Peter and James not being in Galatia and much of what he reported having no witness but himself. Clarke restricts it to his having seen only Peter and James, Ellicott to the extent of his relations with the elder disciples. Calvin uses it to lay down a rule: an oath is lawful only on weighty occasions and is an appeal to the judgment-seat of God. Luther draws another lesson — Paul was in such contempt among his own Galatians that he had to swear he was telling the truth, and if that happened to an apostle, we need not wonder at the like. Gill lists what the oath covers and notes that the charge sworn against was precisely that he had his gospel from men.
21:
Three voices are occupied with squaring these verses against Acts, and each does it differently. Clarke traces the route — Damascus, the basket over the wall, Jerusalem, then Caesarea and Tarsus when the plot was discovered — and concludes that the two accounts agree. Barnes notices what is missing, the dispute with the Hellenists, and says Paul omitted it as immaterial to his point. Ellicott observes that the order of the two names cannot be the order of the journey, since Paul sailed to Tarsus in Cilicia and only afterwards went to Antioch in Syria; a man reviewing his past at a distance speaks in this general way, so it is unnecessary to invent an unrecorded visit and still more gratuitous to find a contradiction. Robertson agrees that the statement matches the history. Gill fills in the story at length, down to Barnabas going to Tarsus to look for him.

The point of saying he was unknown by face is drawn out by Gill: it forestalls the objection that if Paul had not learned the gospel from the apostles he might have had it from the Judean churches. Barnes and Robertson note that Judea here is distinguished from Jerusalem, and Ellicott presses the phrase's incidental value — it points to the spread and early organisation of the Church within ten years of the ascension. He takes which were in Christ for more than a label: the churches stood in the same direct and personal relation to Christ as their head, and his presence diffused among them made them one. Clarke keeps to the point, that he was converted elsewhere and had preached in no congregation of that country.

On the report that reached them, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the tense is continuous — they were hearing, from time to time — and differ over the noun: Robertson takes the faith for the gospel, while Ellicott says it is not yet the body of Christian doctrine, still forming rather than formed, but the single cardinal doctrine of faith in Christ. Calvin stops at the verb instead, with a qualification the others do not make: to say that Paul destroyed the faith does not mean faith can actually be destroyed, only that he lessened its influence on weak minds — and it is the will rather than the deed that the word expresses.

The closing sentence is read the same way by two very different men. Calvin says the praise proves his ministry was approved, and turns it into a warning about how the Lord's saints ought to be regarded: such is our depravity that when we see men adorned with God's gifts we worship them as gods, forgetting the giver. Ellicott says almost the same, calling the verse the proper attitude of Christian hero-worship — an eminent Christian is a city set on a hill, but the admiration he attracts does not rest in him and becomes an occasion of praise to God. Gill finds a reproach in it: churches that had never seen Paul glorified God for him, while the Galatians, to whom he had preached fully, turned away. Barnes reads it as conciliation, showing he had the confidence of the churches in the land held to be the source of ecclesiastical authority. Luther makes it an appeal to witnesses — not Damascus and Arabia only but the whole church of Judea testifies that he preached the faith he once persecuted, glorifying God not for any teaching of circumcision but for the preaching of faith. Clarke draws the sharpest conclusion: Paul owed them nothing and all to God, and was brought into the ministry by no rite the Church has ever used, since neither bishop nor presbyter ever laid hands on him — where many since have been more anxious to show that they were appointed by man than by God, human credentials being easier to display.
